title: Posidonius and the tides
hookLine: a Stoic scientist who studied the tides and the moon

cards: Stand on a beach long enough and the sea moves without asking you. Water creeps up the sand, then slides away, twice a day, later each day, higher at some times of the month than others. Today an app gives the times.

More than two thousand years ago, a philosopher traveled to the far western edge of the known world, to the Atlantic coast of Spain, and spent days watching the water come and go. He wanted to know why.

teach.b: First, the man. Posidonius came from Apamea in Syria, studied under Panaetius, and ran his own Stoic school on the island of Rhodes. Cicero came to hear him lecture; the general Pompey visited him too.
By ancient standards he was a scientist as much as a philosopher: history, geography, astronomy, weather, all of it. Second, the tides.

The geographer Strabo reports that Posidonius stayed at Gades, today's Cádiz, watching the ocean, and connected the rising and falling of the water to the moon: a daily rhythm, a monthly one with the moon's phases, and a yearly one.
He didn't have Newton's gravity. But he saw the pattern, and he saw that the sea and the sky were linked. Third, why a Stoic would care.

The Stoics taught that the universe is one living whole, its parts bound together. They called that bond sympatheia, a feeling-together. For Posidonius, the moon moving the sea wasn't just a fact about water.
It was a sign that the world hangs together, that what happens in one part touches the others. Fourth, what to take from it. Studying nature wasn't a hobby beside his philosophy; it was part of it.
Close attention to the moon, the water, the weather was a way of seeing the order the Stoics praised.

teach.h: ATTENTION AS A KIND OF PRACTICE.
teach.b: Watching the tides was, for him, a kind of practice.
Not everyone today shares his belief in a living cosmos. But anyone can look up and notice the connections.

how: Historians of science count Posidonius among the ancient students of the tides, and readers of the Stoics see in his work the school's belief that the universe is one connected whole.

practice: Breathe in and out like a small tide: in, the water comes up the sand; out, it slides back.
Then picture tonight's sky, and the same moon Posidonius watched over Gades, wherever it is right now, pulling very gently at every ocean on earth.
You don't have to believe anything about it; just notice that you belong to a world where far things touch near things.

wordCard.voice: Sympatheia. The Stoic bond tying the whole cosmos together, which Posidonius saw in how the moon moves the sea. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: sympathy, a feeling-together. The Stoic bond tying all parts of the cosmos, which Posidonius saw in the moon and tides.

carryVoice: Your line: the moon and tides. To a Stoic, the whole world hangs together. Until tomorrow.
